newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir aborts redocking after computer problem.
newsitem.headline: Mir aborts redocking after computer problem.

text.p: The crippled Mir space station on Sunday suddenly delayed a planned docking with its cargo ship because of a computer programming error, space officials said.

The delay was the latest in a series of setbacks that have sent Russia's orbiting station lurching from crisis to crisis, and raised the possibility of another delay in vital repairs planned for Wednesday.

"The necessary baseline data -- which guides the Progress (cargo ship) towards the station -- turned out to be loaded incorrectly," Mission Control flight director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters. "The onboard machine recognised this and gave us an accident warning."
Viktor Blagov, deputy flight director, told Reuters the computer problems arose about three hours before Mir's scheduled 5.54 p.m. (1354 GMT) redocking with the seven-metre-long (23 feet) Progress.
"There is no danger. We are now studying the situation and are planning this procedure for tomorrow," he said.

The manoeuvre was to repeat a procedure carried out on June 25, when a different Progress vehicle docking with Mir collided with the station's Spektr module, causing a major loss of power in the worst accident of the space station's 11-year history.
On Sunday, the crew began the procedure in automatic rather than manual pilot as in June, and apparently the computer recognised a problem ground controllers did not see.
"At first we didn't understand this," Solovyov said. "Another matter is why all the tests we are carrying out on Earth...didn't recognise this."

On Saturday, Vasily Tsibliyev, the cosmonaut at the controls during the June accident, said money woes kept the ailing space station from being properly supplied. "Unfortunately, many things we need on the station just aren't there," he said.

"It all derives from earth, from our economy, our affairs, our poor lives. Because even that equipment needed to live aboard the station that we requested to be sent... it just doesn't exist on earth," he told reporters.

Solovyov said the problem on Sunday was purely technical and had nothing to do with Russia's financial woes. Flight engineers would easily correct the problem by sending new data to Progress and slightly changing its direction, he said.

Blagov said the problem would likely delay by one day plans to repair Spektr. But Solovyov said the effort to reattach cables into Spektr to beef up Mir's energy supply would still take place on Wednesday as planned.
The Russian cosmonauts who will make the Spektr repairs, commander Anatoly Solovyov and flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov, had planned a dress rehearsal on Monday wearing spacesuits.

Progress delivered oxygen, food, water and tools to Mir on July 7 and is now filled mostly with garbage. Space officials said redocking a trash-filled module helps Mir by providing balance for the station and by protecting the hatch from prolonged solar exposure.
It undocked on August 6 to make room for a Soyuz spaceship bringing cosmonauts Solovyov and Vinogradov.

Mir has faced an expanding host of problems in recent months in addition to the June 25 crash. Last month the former crew mistakely unplugged a vital computer, sending the ship spinning in disorientation for a day.

When Solovyov and Vinogradov arrived at Mir earlier this month, they had to make a sudden manual docking. And when Tsibliyev and his flight engineer returned to Earth on Thursday, a booster rocket that should have eased their landing failed.
